extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, academic researchers, journal editors, and people interested in academic publishing models
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and considerations for evaluating or designing academic (mathematics) journals and publishing models, especially gold open-access / author-pays proposals. Focuses on affordability, sustainability, ethics, certification role, and practical implementation details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affordability for authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Can authors (including grad students, postdocs, and unfunded researchers) realistically pay the proposed publication charge (e.g. $750)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments: “Why would an author pay money to make his work available for free?”; “$750 is nearly half my monthly take home pay.” Consider waivers, departmental disparities, and the effect on those without discretionary funds. Assess whether APCs create undue financial burdens on typical authors in the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional subscription and per-paper cost comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare total institutional/library spending per published paper (subscriptions) with proposed per-paper APCs or other charges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: computing a ratio between department subscription spend and number of papers (e.g. “at least 1300€ per published paper”); estimate what subscribers currently pay per article. Use these comparisons when justifying APC levels or alternative funding mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scalability of volunteer-run free journals
rubrics_metrics.description: Can a volunteer-run, free journal model scale to cover the whole system given finite scientist time?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concern: “they rely a lot on the time of scientists, which is neither free nor infinite.” Evaluate administrative burden, editor/manager availability, and whether the volunteer pipeline exists for many more journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value added by copy-editing and typesetting
rubrics_metrics.description: Is professional copy-editing/typesetting worth the cost, and should it be applied to all papers or selectively?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Viewpoints: “I feel copy-editing is a good thing to keep at least for the papers that are likely to be read by a lot of people.” Consider whether drop-in of copy-editing saves costs, whether authors can supply typeset-ready files, and which papers merit full production services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distributional fairness and impact on early-career researchers
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the model disadvantage early-career, unfunded, or low-salary researchers who submit frequently or cannot access institutional funds?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Points raised: burden falls on those who submit borderline papers (often junior researchers); “burden of paying for publishing would be pushed onto those who frequently submit... young people without permanent positions.” Include waiver policies and alternative funding to avoid inequitable effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of certification/quality-stamp function
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the model protect the journal’s role as a stamp of scientific credibility rather than turning that stamp into something for sale?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concerns: “The option of putting these stamps of credibility up for sale is wrong.” Evaluate safeguards that maintain editorial independence and rigor rather than monetizing acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical acceptability of author-pays model
rubrics_metrics.description: Is asking authors to pay for publication ethically defensible given the research funding and the role of public support?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong views: “It is ethically wrong regardless of math.” Consider arguments about public funding, taxpayer access, and principles around who should bear publishing costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community consultation and governance
rubrics_metrics.description: Were major changes (e.g. launching an APC-charging journal) discussed openly with the community before implementation?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complaint: presented as a result not a suggestion; “faced with such fundamental decisions without any open discussion beforehand.” Models should include transparent community consultation and governance processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and justification of APC amount
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a clear breakdown and justification for the proposed APC (e.g. how $750 was computed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requests: “I would like to see much more justification for the $750 price tag.” Include itemized costs (production, staff, platform, overhead) and evidence supporting time/cost estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fee waiver and equity policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the journal offer waivers or reduced charges for authors from developing countries or those without funding?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FAQ note: “fee waivers available for authors from developing countries.” Evaluate scope, eligibility, and transparency of waiver policies to ensure global inclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perverse incentives linking revenue to acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the funding model create incentives to accept more papers to increase revenue (e.g. pay-to-publish pressure)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning: “the more the papers accepted, the better (for the ‘cashier’)”. Require structural safeguards (separate editorial and financial control, capped APC-driven revenue dependence) to prevent conflict of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferred funding mechanism (institutional vs per-paper)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is funding via institutions or consortia preferable to per-paper charges levied on authors?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: “Funding it via institutions would be better than on a paper by paper basis.” Consider consortia, library subscriptions repurposed for APCs, or institutional agreements to reduce individual burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic feasibility vs acceptance/rejection dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: What acceptance/rejection rates are economically required for the proposed APC to sustain the journal, and are those rates compatible with fairness?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: to break even the journal might need to reject 1/2 to 3/4 of submissions depending on processing cost assumptions. Assess whether required quotas would distort editorial fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of author control over venue choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the model shift control from authors to administrators (e.g. departmental budget limits), reducing authors' freedom to choose where to submit?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concern: “This model shifts the control over publications from the authors to administrators.” Evaluate how institutional budget constraints, approval processes, or limited funds affect submission decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corruption and exploitation risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the model create incentives or opportunities for corrupt practices or exploitation (e.g. cherry-picking, nepotism) in publishing decisions?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comment: “There is too much motivation in this model for corruption which means corruption will happen.” Include governance safeguards and transparent auditing to mitigate risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment of payment with the consumer of the service
rubrics_metrics.description: Who should bear the publishing cost — the author, the author's institution, or the reader — aligned with who benefits from the service?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Debate: “it seems natural to align the point of payment with the person consuming the service (or more precisely, the institution of the person consuming the service).” Consider certification-as-service to authors vs dissemination-as-service to readers when choosing funding flows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of preprint servers and community review
rubrics_metrics.description: Promote use of arXiv and consider platforms for open, signed reviews of arXiv papers as complementary certification/dissemination mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggestions: arXiv-like platform collecting signed reviews; “ArXiv is a great step forward.” Evaluate whether such infrastructure can reduce reliance on paid production or certification services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for unpaid editorial/referee labor
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that editors and referees are typically unpaid and factor this into cost, sustainability, and ethical evaluation of charging models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation: “editors and referees are not paid for their services.” If most peer-review labor is volunteer, justify APCs by enumerating paid services that truly require external expenditure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding undermining wider community boycotts or reforms
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether partnering with commercial publishers or adopting certain models undermines broader community actions (e.g. Elsevier boycott).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concern: adoption of commercial OA models could be perceived as conflicting with boycott aims. Consider reputational effects and alignment with community initiatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encouraging diversity of publication models
rubrics_metrics.description: Support a plurality of models (free electronic journals, institutional funding, low-cost APCs) rather than forcing a single approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Viewpoints: “there is certainly room for several models and a urge to experiment.” Evaluate how the proposed model fits alongside truly free journals and lower-cost alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market viability of micro-pay-per-reader schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether charging small per-reader fees (e.g. $2–$4 per reader) is a viable route to remunerate authors or sustain journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skepticism: at $4/paper many papers would have very few readers and not generate sustainable revenue. Model market demand realistically (typical readership per article) before relying on micro-payments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear revenue/value proposition beyond reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify what the journal is selling and to whom (production services, certification, brand/reputation), with a clear target market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question: “What and to whom are they going to sell here?” A viable business model requires an explicit product and buyers — e.g., reliable certification for hiring/promotion committees or production services for broader readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright and author rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the journal require authors to assign copyright, or allow them to retain rights (green OA compatibility, author-friendly licenses)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive note: moving away from requiring authors to sign over copyright was welcomed. Prefer policies that let authors keep rights and enable self-archiving where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Care when experimenting with models that have real-world effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between small-scale technical experiments and policy changes that have ethical and practical consequences; treat the latter with community oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: “It is one thing to experiment with, say, using MathJax on your blog, but it is another thing to take action in the real world... Action which has moral and practical significance cannot be excused as experimentation.” Use cautious pilots with evaluation and stakeholder input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about reputation-leveraging and conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Be explicit about how editorial board prominence (names like Cambridge, Gowers, Tao) is used to build reputation and whether that creates commercial leverage or conflicts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation: some authors worry that reputation is being used to ‘sell’ credibility. Disclose motivations, financial arrangements with publishers, and any potential conflicts tied to reputational leverage.
